_contract: The architecture DEBT that src/aadistill carries today, listed site by site so it is countable. This is not permission: each rule may only shrink, and tests/architecture/test_core_boundaries.py fails both when a new site appears and when a listed site is fixed without lowering the count. Every entry is a piece of the migration the maintainer has asked for.
derived_by: scripts/architecture/inventory.py (AST; docstrings excluded, comments absent), keyed by tests/architecture/test_core_boundaries.py::_violations
identity: path::owner::sha256(offending value)[:10]. The discriminator names the offending CONTENT, so a site keeps its identity when unrelated code moves, and a SECOND violation inside an already-listed owner is a new identity rather than a duplicate that de-duplicates away. Entries may repeat: multiplicity is part of the debt and is compared as a multiset.

_count_change_at_the_migration.why_some_counts_rose: The identity became more precise, not the tree worse. The previous identity was file+owner and was de-duplicated, so every violation after the first inside one function was invisible -- 4 baselined family-access owners were really 37 accesses, and 13 path-literal owners were really 37 literals. Comparing LIKE FOR LIKE, on the old identity, every rule improved or held across the migration.
_count_change_at_the_migration.reading: [before the migration, after], counted the OLD way

_accepted_revision_meaning: the commit whose allowance this one may not exceed. Growing a list means committing the wider baseline and then pointing this field at it, so the widening is a diff of its own rather than a line inside the change that wanted it.
_remaining_debt: NONE. Every rule is at zero, including path_literals -- the last one, and the reason this file still had an allow list. What it held was the reusable core naming (a) which log a phase's accounting lives in and (b) which scripts the session runner executes. Both are now supplied by the caller: the accounting paths by scripts/experiments/phase_b/post_freeze.py and scripts/experiments/phase_c1/pod_environment.py, the executables by SessionSpec.commands (an ExecutionCommands with no defaults). An empty allow list makes this a plain refusal rather than a ratchet, which is what a ratchet is for.
